records.sourceFile: Association between intra and inter-limb strength asymmetry with sprint kinematics and force-velocity profile in youth team athletes.pdf

paper.citation: İnce İ, Tortu E. Association between intra and inter-limb strength asymmetry with sprint kinematics and force-velocity profile in youth team athletes. The Knee. 2025;52:99-107.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined relationships among isokinetic knee-strength asymmetry, sprint kinematics, and sprint force-velocity characteristics in 74 youth athletes from football, volleyball, and handball.
paper.tldr: Strength-asymmetry measures showed only weak-to-moderate, metric-dependent relationships with sprint variables. Most athletes were below 15% asymmetry, but some reached 42%; neither value creates a universal performance, injury-risk, or training threshold.
paper.methods: Athletes completed two sessions 48 hours apart, including anthropometry, sprint testing, Optojump kinematic analysis, Samozino force-velocity profiling, and isokinetic knee-flexor and knee-extensor testing at 60 and 180 degrees per second. Standard percentage-difference equations quantified asymmetry.
paper.findings: Associations between intra- and inter-limb strength asymmetry and sprint measures ranged from weak to moderate and changed with the strength and sprint variable examined. Group asymmetry was usually below 15%, but individual values were highly variable and reached 42%.
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot show whether asymmetry causes performance or injury outcomes. A mixed-sport youth sample, multiple test speeds and definitions, and no prospective injury or intervention follow-up prevent causal interpretation or a universal cutoff.
paper.practicalImplications: Standardize the muscle action, speed, limb comparison, and sprint metric before monitoring change. Investigate large or changing values in the context of the athlete's own strength, sprint mechanics, symptoms, and training history.
paper.athleteDev: Develop bilateral and unilateral strength and sprint skill while judging progress from multiple performance measures. Do not devote training to reducing an asymmetry percentage unless the underlying limb capacity or sport function also warrants attention.
paper.rtp: During rehabilitation, reproduce the same test conditions and examine absolute limb capacity alongside symmetry, symptoms, sprint progression, and sport tasks. A 15% boundary is not a validated clearance rule.

records.sourceFile: The impact of intrinsic foot muscle strengthening exercises in asymptomatic athletes with normal foot structure - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Ahmed M, Zaki S, Alam MF, et al. The impact of intrinsic foot muscle strengthening exercises in asymptomatic athletes with normal foot structure: A systematic review. Clinical Epidemiology and Global Health. 2024;27:101597.
paper.abstract: This systematic review evaluated intrinsic-foot-muscle strengthening in asymptomatic athletes with normal foot structure. Four heterogeneous studies were included, preventing meta-analysis.
paper.tldr: The small evidence base suggested improvements in intrinsic-foot strength and some morphological, motor, and propulsive-force outcomes, but running economy did not improve and one study found no change in arch stiffness. Results are promising but too heterogeneous and bias-prone for a guaranteed performance or prevention claim.
paper.methods: Six databases were searched for eligible athlete studies, and the Cochrane tool was used to assess risk of bias. Four studies were synthesized qualitatively because protocols, measurement units, and outcomes could not be pooled.
paper.findings: All four studies reported improved intrinsic-foot strength, with some favorable changes in foot morphology, clinician-rated motor performance, subjective function, and vertical running propulsive force. Running economy was unchanged, and one eight-week intervention did not alter medial-longitudinal-arch stiffness.
paper.limitations: Only four heterogeneous studies were available, interventions were only roughly comparable, outcome units differed, and risk of bias was present. Healthy athletes with normal feet do not establish treatment efficacy for painful or pathological feet or injury prevention.
paper.practicalImplications: Intrinsic-foot work can be a low-cost accessory when foot capacity is relevant, but select outcomes deliberately and reassess them. Do not promise improved running economy, arch stiffness, or fewer injuries from short-foot exercises alone.
paper.athleteDev: Progress foot-muscle control and loading within a broader program that includes calf strength, balance, jumping, running, footwear, and sport exposure. Keep the dosage tolerable and judge value by the athlete's targeted function.
paper.rtp: For foot or lower-limb rehabilitation, these healthy-athlete findings provide a possible exercise option rather than a clinical protocol. Progress symptoms, tissue loading, whole-limb capacity, running, and sport tasks before clearance.

records.sourceFile: Prophylactic knee bracing in offensive linemen of the National Football League - A retrospective analysis of usage trends, player performance, a.pdf

paper.citation: Ackerman DR, Ptasinski AM, Edmond T, et al. Prophylactic knee bracing in offensive linemen of the National Football League: A retrospective analysis of usage trends, player performance, and major knee injury. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;11(8):23259671231191767.
paper.abstract: This retrospective cohort analysis compared major knee injury and Pro Football Focus performance grades in NFL offensive-lineman seasons with and without observed bilateral prophylactic knee-brace use from 2014 through 2020.
paper.tldr: Brace use was associated with fewer major knee injuries (0.013 versus 0.049 per player; P=.04) and no cumulative performance-grade difference, even as use declined from 16.3% to 5.6%. Nonrandom brace choice, unequal groups, unknown prior injury, and public-data classification prevent a causal conclusion.
paper.methods: Offensive linemen with at least 200 regular-season snaps were classified as bracers or nonbracers using public images and game video. Public injury reports identified knee injuries causing missed games, and season-level Pro Football Focus grades represented performance.
paper.findings: Bracers had a lower cumulative rate of major knee injury than nonbracers, and isolated medial-collateral-ligament injury was the most common event among nonbracers. Cumulative and most season-specific performance grades did not differ significantly, while brace use declined across the seven seasons.
paper.limitations: Brace exposure was self-selected and groups were imbalanced. Prior injury, baseline knee risk, player skill, brace type, fit, and compliance could not be fully controlled, while brace and injury identification depended on public sources and performance grades may miss relevant task effects.
paper.practicalImplications: Consider prophylactic bracing through shared medical, equipment, performance, and player decision-making for offensive linemen. Discuss fit, comfort, role demands, prior injury, and uncertainty instead of presenting the observed association as guaranteed protection.
paper.athleteDev: If bracing is used, integrate it during practice so stance, footwork, leverage, and conditioning adapt to the equipment. Maintain strength, mobility, technique, and exposure management rather than treating the brace as the sole prevention strategy.
paper.rtp: This study concerns prophylaxis, not postinjury clearance. A brace may be one risk-management component after knee injury, but readiness still requires medical stability, strength, function, football movement, contact tolerance, and position-specific work.

records.sourceFile: A comparison of rolling averages vs discrete time epochs for assessing the worst-case scenario locomotor demands of professional soccer match-play.pdf

paper.citation: Fereday K, Hills SP, Russell M, et al. A comparison of rolling averages versus discrete time epochs for assessing the worst-case scenario locomotor demands of professional soccer match-play. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2020;23(8):764-769.
paper.abstract: This descriptive observational study compared fixed epochs with rolling averages for estimating peak total-distance and high-speed-running demands in 25 professional outfield soccer players across 28 matches.
paper.tldr: Fixed epochs underestimated rolling-average peak demand by roughly 7-10% for total distance and 12-25% for high-speed distance. Peak values also changed substantially with window length, position, starting status, and match context, so the calculation method must travel with the number.
paper.methods: Players from one English Championship club wore 10-Hz tracking systems. Relative total and high-speed distance were calculated with fixed and rolling windows from 60 to 600 seconds, and mixed models examined epoch, position, starting status, result, location, formation, and time of day.
paper.findings: Rolling 60-second peaks averaged 190.1 m/min for total distance and 59.5 m/min for high-speed distance, falling to 120.9 and 14.2 m/min at 600 seconds. Fixed windows consistently returned lower values, and several positional and match-context effects were present.
paper.limitations: One club and 28 matches limit generalization, while estimates depend on the device, speed threshold, processing, window, and tactical context. Peak locomotor values omit technical, tactical, collision, acceleration, and individual physiological demands and do not identify an optimal training dose.
paper.practicalImplications: Use rolling averages when the goal is to capture true peak passages, and report the window, threshold, device, and processing rules. Build club- and position-specific distributions instead of copying a published number into practice design.
paper.athleteDev: Expose athletes progressively to short intense passages and longer sustained demands that reflect their role. Use peak-demand data as a planning reference while preserving technical and tactical representativeness.
paper.rtp: Compare reintegration exposure with the athlete's own role-specific rolling-window demands. Progress both intensity and duration, but do not use one peak running value as a standalone clearance criterion.

records.sourceFile: Accumulative weekly load in a professional soccer team - With special reference to match playing time and game position.pdf

paper.citation: Casamichana D, Martín-García A, Gómez Díaz A, et al. Accumulative weekly load in a professional football team: With special reference to match playing time and game position. Biology of Sport. 2022;39(1):115-124.
paper.abstract: This observational study compared GPS-derived weekly external load in 24 professional reserve-squad soccer players according to match-minute group and playing position.
paper.tldr: Players completing more match minutes generally accumulated greater weekly total, high-speed, sprint, and high-metabolic-load distance. Match participation can create predictable exposure gaps, but this one-team study did not test a universal compensatory top-up dose or show that top-ups improve outcomes.
paper.methods: Training and official-match GPS data were accumulated for total distance, high-speed and sprint distance, high-metabolic-load distance, and high-intensity accelerations and decelerations. Weeks were compared across 90-minute, more-than-60, less-than-60, and zero-minute match groups and by position.
paper.findings: Greater match participation produced higher weekly exposure for most variables, particularly total and high-metabolic-load distance and, for full-match players, high-speed and sprint distance. Position-specific patterns were evident, although relative-to-match comparisons showed less positional variation.
paper.limitations: The sample came from one professional reserve squad. Indoor work and internal-load measures were absent, and broad match-minute groups masked exposure differences such as 61 versus 89 minutes. No injury, adaptation, or performance response to compensatory training was tested.
paper.practicalImplications: Use match minutes and position as an early flag for underexposure, then quantify the athlete's actual week and deliver individualized top-up work that targets the missing qualities without compromising recovery.
paper.athleteDev: Protect adequate high-speed, sprint, and total-volume exposure for nonstarters across the season. Build these opportunities into a consistent development plan rather than waiting for match selection to supply all conditioning.
paper.rtp: Match-minute groups can contextualize the demands an athlete is missing during reintegration. Progress external load and internal response toward individual role demands while accounting for tissue status and next-day recovery.

records.sourceFile: Are elite soccer teams preseason training sessions associated with fewer in-season injuries - A 15-year analysis from the UEFA Elite Club Injury Study.pdf

paper.citation: Ekstrand J, Spreco A, Windt J, Khan KM. Are elite soccer teams' preseason training sessions associated with fewer in-season injuries? A 15-year analysis from the UEFA Elite Club Injury Study. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;48(3):723-729.
paper.abstract: This team-level epidemiological study examined whether the number of preseason training sessions was associated with competitive-season injury outcomes across 244 team-seasons from 44 elite European soccer clubs.
paper.tldr: Every 10 additional preseason sessions was associated with lower injury burden and severe-injury incidence plus slightly better training attendance and match availability. Model fit was only 1.3-3.2%, so session count explained little of the variation and should not be interpreted as a causal dose.
paper.methods: UEFA Elite Club Injury Study data spanning up to 15 seasons were analyzed with separate linear regressions. Preseason session count was related to in-season injury burden, severe-injury incidence, overall injury incidence, training attendance, and match availability.
paper.findings: Ten additional sessions corresponded to 22 fewer layoff days per 1000 hours, 0.18 fewer severe injuries per 1000 hours, 1.4 percentage points greater training attendance, and 1.0 point greater match availability. Four of five outcomes favored more sessions.
paper.limitations: The team-level observational design cannot separate session count from player availability, roster quality, medical systems, travel, coaching, content, or resilience. Low adjusted R-squared values show that most injury variation was unexplained, and the association does not establish an optimal number or intensity.
paper.practicalImplications: Protect enough preseason time for progressive preparation and reduce avoidable travel or scheduling erosion. Judge preseason quality through participation, content, progression, and response rather than chasing a session total.
paper.athleteDev: Use preseason to rebuild exposure systematically across strength, running, football, and recovery demands. Preserve individual modification while avoiding unnecessary underpreparation for athletes who can train.
paper.rtp: Athletes returning during preseason need an individualized progression, not automatic completion of the team session count. Track the relevant loading content, function, symptoms, and football exposure before full availability.

records.sourceFile: Introducing the Novel Deceleration Threshold Method - Comparative Reliability to Previous Sprint Deceleration Analysis Methods in Team‐Sport Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: West MA, Compton HR, Dascombe BJ, Secomb JL. Introducing the novel deceleration threshold method: Comparative reliability to previous sprint deceleration analysis methods in team-sport athletes. European Journal of Sport Science. 2025;25(4):e12278.
paper.abstract: This methodological study compared three analysis methods for preplanned sprint deceleration testing in 20 team-sport participants using motorized linear-encoder data collected across two days.
paper.tldr: A threshold-based start point combined with the average of the best two trials produced excellent interday reliability for time to stop, distance to stop, and average deceleration. That reliability is protocol specific and does not establish criterion validity, injury prediction, or transfer to multidirectional play.
paper.methods: Ten women and 10 men performed three maximal 30-m sprint-to-stop trials on two testing days. Set-distance, peak-velocity, and novel deceleration-threshold analyses produced time-to-stop, distance-to-stop, and average-deceleration metrics, with reliability tested using ICC, CV, and standard error.
paper.findings: The threshold method using the average of the best two trials returned interday ICC and CV values of .93 and 6.4% for time to stop, .97 and 5.3% for distance to stop, and .92 and 7.1% for average deceleration.
paper.limitations: The small mixed sample, one linear task, motorized encoder, customized processing, and two-day design constrain generalization. The study did not compare against a criterion measure or test responsiveness, multidirectional deceleration, sport performance, or injury outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: If adopting the test, reproduce the threshold definition, equipment, filtering, 30-m protocol, and average-of-best-two rule. Interpret change against device- and metric-specific error.
paper.athleteDev: Use reliable linear testing to profile stopping strategy alongside strength, sprinting, multidirectional movement, and sport practice. Train braking capacity progressively without treating one laboratory metric as the whole quality.
paper.rtp: The protocol may document recovery of repeatable linear deceleration performance, but clearance also requires symptoms, tissue capacity, directional variety, unplanned tasks, fatigue tolerance, and representative sport exposure.

records.sourceFile: Unilateral or bilateral standing broad jumps - Which jump type provides inter-limb asymmetries with a higher reliability.pdf

paper.citation: Pérez-Castilla A, García-Ramos A, Janicijevic D, et al. Unilateral or bilateral standing broad jumps: Which jump type provides inter-limb asymmetries with a higher reliability? Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2021;20:317-327.
paper.abstract: This methodological study compared between-session reliability of force-platform performance and inter-limb-asymmetry variables from unilateral and bilateral standing broad jumps in 24 amateur basketball players.
paper.tldr: Most raw single-limb performance variables were acceptably reliable in both jump variants, but derived asymmetry values were not: ICCs ranged from -.40 to .58 and the favored limb was usually inconsistent. Reliable limb measurements do not automatically create a reliable asymmetry score.
paper.methods: Twelve women and 12 men completed two identical sessions of four unilateral and two bilateral standing broad jumps. Dual force platforms measured limb-specific force, velocity, power, and impulse; percentage-difference and bilateral-asymmetry equations generated asymmetry metrics.
paper.findings: Most performance-variable CVs were 3.65-9.81%, with some force and power variables reaching 10.00-15.46%. Asymmetry reliability was unacceptable and direction agreement was mostly slight to fair, with only isolated metrics showing moderate agreement.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, amateur, and limited to basketball and two sessions. Results depend on the jump variant, metric, and asymmetry equation, while no injury, performance, intervention, or clinical outcome was evaluated.
paper.practicalImplications: Track absolute performance for each limb and its measurement error before calculating asymmetry. Confirm an unusual result across repeated sessions and relevant tasks rather than reacting to one percentage.
paper.athleteDev: Use unilateral and bilateral broad jumps to describe horizontal-jump qualities, not to impose a stable weak-side identity. Base training priorities on repeatable capacity deficits and sport needs.
paper.rtp: A broad-jump asymmetry percentage should not determine clearance. Use repeated absolute limb performance alongside symptoms, strength, landing and propulsion skill, running, and sport-specific tolerance.

records.sourceFile: Validity of the Hawkin Dynamics wireless dual force platform system against a piezoelectric laboratory grade system for vertical countermovement jump variables.pdf

paper.citation: Dos'Santos T, Evans DT, Read DB. Validity of the Hawkin Dynamics wireless dual force platform system against a piezoelectric laboratory grade system for vertical countermovement jump variables. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(6):1144-1148.
paper.abstract: This criterion-comparison study placed Hawkin Dynamics wireless dual force platforms directly over Kistler laboratory platforms while two recreational male soccer players performed 25 countermovement jumps each.
paper.tldr: Across 16 countermovement-jump variables, system differences were no more than 3.4% and 15 variables correlated .977-1.000, but fixed bias affected six variables and proportional bias affected 10. The platforms appear suitable for the tested uses, yet values should not be assumed interchangeable.
paper.methods: Vertical ground-reaction force was collected simultaneously from stacked Hawkin Dynamics and Kistler systems during 50 jumps. Sixteen outcome and strategy variables were compared for fixed and proportional bias, percentage difference, and correlation.
paper.findings: Near-perfect to perfect correlations were observed for 15 variables. Fixed bias affected braking power, mean propulsion force, time to takeoff, flight time, and body weight measures; proportional bias affected multiple propulsion, braking, timing, power, and body-weight variables despite small overall percentage differences.
paper.limitations: Only two participants generated the 50 repeated observations in one session, limiting independence and generalization. High correlation does not prove agreement, and the design did not assess between-session reliability, longitudinal sensitivity, broader populations, or device interchangeability.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the Hawkin system consistently and establish its own baselines, error, and change rules for each variable. Avoid mixing historical Kistler values or assuming small changes are biological when bias or noise could explain them.
paper.athleteDev: Force-platform data can clarify jump outcome and strategy when testing is standardized. Use it to support, not replace, strength, power, movement, and sport-performance assessment.
paper.rtp: Device-consistent jump trends may contribute to rehabilitation monitoring, but this validation study supplies no return-to-sport cutoff. Combine results with symptoms, strength, function, and graded sport exposure.

records.sourceFile: Associations between skeletal muscle mass, fat-free mass, and saliva osmolality - A cross-sectional study.pdf

paper.citation: Winter IP, Burdin J, Wilson PB. Associations between skeletal muscle mass, fat-free mass, and saliva osmolality: A cross-sectional study. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2026;36(4):508-513.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study evaluated whether skeletal muscle mass or fat-free mass was associated with portable-device saliva osmolality in 72 adults.
paper.tldr: Neither skeletal muscle mass nor fat-free mass was meaningfully associated with saliva osmolality before or after adjustment; correlations were only .10 and .08. This reduces concern about one potential body-composition confounder but does not validate a single saliva value as a complete hydration assessment.
paper.methods: Forty-two men and 30 women completed bioelectrical-impedance body-composition measurement and provided two saliva samples three to five minutes apart for MX3 osmolality testing. Models adjusted for age, sex, four-hour fluid intake, and sampling time.
paper.findings: Unadjusted associations for muscle mass and fat-free mass were nonsignificant, as were adjusted models. Spearman correlations with saliva osmolality were small and nonsignificant at .10 and .08, respectively.
paper.limitations: This convenience sample was not an athlete validation cohort, body composition was estimated by bioelectrical impedance, and paired saliva samples were collected within minutes. Cross-sectional null associations do not establish diagnostic validity, responsiveness, or decision thresholds across hydration states.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not automatically correct saliva osmolality for muscle mass in similar adults, but interpret it with recent intake, environment, symptoms, body-mass change, urine measures, and individual trends.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes that hydration assessment is contextual and that one portable reading is not a verdict. Build individualized drinking routines around training demand, climate, access, and observed fluid loss.
paper.rtp: Saliva osmolality may supplement monitoring during illness, heat exposure, or rehabilitation, but it is not a clearance test. Resolve clinical hydration concerns with medical assessment and corroborating evidence.

records.sourceFile: The effects of integrative neuromuscular training on injury risk and athletic performance in athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Jiang T, Zhang M, Wang Z, Wang P. The effects of integrative neuromuscular training on injury risk and athletic performance in athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2026;18(1):115.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized 25 randomized trials involving 10,124 participants to evaluate integrative neuromuscular training for injury risk and jump, sprint, change-of-direction, and dynamic-balance performance.
paper.tldr: Multicomponent neuromuscular training was associated with 27% lower injury risk and moderate-to-large performance improvements, but most outcomes were heterogeneous and most trials had some risk-of-bias concerns. Favorable subgroup and dose patterns are hypotheses, not proof of one best program.
paper.methods: Nine databases were searched through August 31, 2025. Randomized trials were pooled using risk ratios and standardized mean differences, with ROB2, GRADE, publication-bias checks, and subgroup analyses by athlete and intervention characteristics.
paper.findings: Pooled injury risk was .73 (95% CI .58-.91). Standardized mean differences favored training for jump .88, sprint .75, change of direction .97, and dynamic balance .91; subgroup analyses suggested larger effects in some adult, female, football, higher-frequency, and longer-session categories.
paper.limitations: Intervention content, populations, sports, outcomes, and follow-up varied, significant heterogeneity affected most analyses, and most trials had some risk-of-bias concerns. Subgroups cannot establish causal superiority, and the reviewed local source is an unedited early-access manuscript.
paper.practicalImplications: Use structured multicomponent training that combines strength, landing, balance, plyometric, agility, and movement exposure appropriate to the sport. Protect adherence and progression while monitoring whether the chosen program changes its intended outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: Embed neuromuscular development consistently rather than as a brief warm-up campaign. Progress complexity and load with training age and preserve enough high-quality exposure for adaptation.
paper.rtp: Components can support restoration of strength, landing, balance, and change-of-direction capacity, but pooled prevention effects do not define clearance. Rebuild individual deficits and representative sport tolerance before unrestricted return.

records.sourceFile: The Relationship Between Training Load and Injury in Athletes- A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Eckard TG, Padua DA, Hearn DW, Pexa BS, Frank BS. The relationship between training load and injury in athletes: A systematic review. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(8):1929-1961.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined prospective relationships between training load and musculoskeletal injury across athlete, military, and first-responder populations, including 57 studies published before July 2017.
paper.tldr: Forty-seven studies reported at least partly significant load–injury relationships, with the most consistent evidence for subjective internal load. Direction depended on the metric and timeframe; the review supports thoughtful load monitoring but not a universal safe ratio, cutoff, or individual injury prediction.
paper.methods: Five databases were searched for prospective studies. Fifty-seven articles underwent Newcastle-Ottawa quality assessment and Oxford evidence grading, followed by narrative synthesis because populations, exposures, timeframes, outcomes, and analyses were heterogeneous.
paper.findings: Forty-seven studies found at least some significant relationship between load and injury. Thirty-six studies were rated good, six fair, and 15 poor; subjective internal-load measures showed the strongest overall support, while both high and low loads could be associated with risk depending on timing and context.
paper.limitations: Most evidence was observational and vulnerable to confounding, reverse causation, exposure misclassification, and inconsistent injury definitions. Heterogeneity prevented a pooled threshold, and statistical associations at group level cannot reliably predict which athlete will be injured.
paper.practicalImplications: Use load data to improve conversations and planning: monitor external exposure, internal response, rapid changes, chronic preparation, schedule, and athlete context together. Avoid automated red-light decisions from one ratio or threshold.
paper.athleteDev: Build durable capacity through progressive, consistent exposure and use monitoring to identify unusual change or underpreparation. The aim is informed adjustment, not keeping every athlete below a single workload number.
paper.rtp: Track rehabilitation and team exposure as context for graded reintegration, but do not infer reinjury probability from one load metric. Combine response to loading with symptoms, function, tissue status, and sport-specific demands.
